identity.title: The Role of Interferons in Regulating and Mediating NK Cell Anti-Tumor Immunity.

content.abstract: Interferons (IFNs) are cytokines critical for natural killer (NK) cell development, activation, cytotoxicity, and anti-tumor function. In this review, we examine how type I and type II IFNs shape NK cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity, with an emphasis on recent advances and their implications for NK cell-based cancer therapy. Although IFNs have traditionally been viewed as immune activating cytokines and biomarkers of effective anti-tumor immunity, emerging evidence suggests that their effects in cancer are highly context dependent. By integrating recent CRISPR screening studies in NK cells, mechanistic analyses of IFN signaling in NK cell therapy, and emerging evidence on IFN-NK cell crosstalk within the tumor microenvironment, we highlight a central paradox: while IFNs can enhance NK cell activation and tumor surveillance, they can also drive dysfunction, tumor immune adaptation, and therapeutic resistance under chronic or dysregulated conditions. This distinction is particularly important in solid tumors, where NK cell therapies continue to face major barriers, including poor tumor infiltration, limited persistence, and suppression by the tumor microenvironment. We propose that IFN signaling may be one underappreciated factor contributing to the highly variable efficacy of NK cell therapy across cancer models. Therefore, IFNs should not be understood simply as pro-inflammatory or anti-tumor signals. Instead, they function as dynamic immune regulators whose effects depend on timing, dose, duration, cellular source, and tumor context. We further discuss the current clinical landscape of IFN-NK therapies, including IFN-alpha and INF-beta drugs, CAR-NK cell therapy, STING agonists, and other rational combination strategies. Future research should develop physiologically relevant and tumor-microenvironment representative model systems to investigate the effects of IFN signaling on NK cell anti-tumor function across distinct tumor types. Coordinated investigation of NK, cytokine, and tumor biology will accelerate clinically actionable strategies that leverage the NK-IFN axis.
